claims.text: At elevated temperatures, FeNiCrCoCu coating wear resistance is governed by formation of a continuous, adherent oxide scale.
The oxide scale reinforces the coating through oxide dispersion strengthening.
The oxide scale reduces direct metal-to-metal contact during sliding wear.
The initial coating is a polycrystalline, fine-grained FeNiCrCoCu thin film on a conventional metal substrate.
Exposure to sliding wear at 600–800 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere promotes protective oxide-scale formation relative to room-temperature wear.
A duplex surface oxide develops, consisting of an outer dense, adherent oxide and an inner transitional layer.
The outer oxide may contain mixed oxides of Fe, Ni, Cr, Co, and Cu.
The inner transitional oxide layer improves interfacial bonding with the metal substrate.
Accelerated high-temperature oxidation produces a continuous oxide scale.
The oxide scale increases hardness through oxide dispersion strengthening.
The oxide scale acts as a self-lubricating barrier that reduces adhesive and abrasive wear.
Improved oxide-to-alloy adhesion prevents premature scale spallation and thereby reduces material loss.
Compared with room-temperature testing, high-temperature testing will produce lower wear rate and friction coefficient and higher surface hardness.
The predicted tribological improvement will coincide with a dense, continuous oxide layer on the worn surface.
At room temperature, limited oxide formation leads to greater plastic deformation and a higher wear rate.
The proposed oxide-controlled mechanism dominates in oxidizing environments between roughly 600 °C and 800 °C.
Below roughly 600 °C, insufficient oxide formation undermines the protective effect.
Above roughly 800 °C, excessive oxidation may cause brittle scale spallation.

contradictions.description: The inner oxide layer is said to bond directly with the metal substrate in one field but to adhere to the underlying alloy in another. For an oxide formed at the coating surface, the immediate underlying material would normally be the FeNiCrCoCu coating rather than the substrate.
